title.en: Climate Action: Taiwan's Path to Net Zero

A2.text: Our summers are getting very long and hot. The world has a big climate problem. We see bad storms and melting ice. Today, let us talk about how we save our planet.

B1.text: Have you noticed that our summers keep getting longer and hotter? This is not your imagination, because our world is facing a real climate crisis. Today I will show you how we fight it.

B2.text: Have you noticed our summers becoming steadily longer and more intense? This is not simply an impression: the planet is in a genuine climate crisis, and melting ice remains an urgent warning we can no longer ignore.

A2.text: What is SDG 13? It means Climate Action. It asks every country to cut dirty air and prepare for disasters. If we do not act now, our cities will be in danger.

B1.text: So what is SDG 13? It is a global call for climate action, and it asks every country to cut carbon and prepare for disasters. The goal is to keep our planet cool.

B2.text: What exactly does SDG 13 demand of us as a country? It is an international call for climate action, requiring every nation to reduce carbon emissions and strengthen disaster resilience before rising temperatures damage our cities permanently.

A2.text: Look at Taiwan. We are a small island, so typhoons and rising seas hurt us easily. Our high-tech factories also use a lot of electricity. How can we help the world?

B1.text: Now think about Taiwan. As a small island, we are easily hurt by typhoons and rising seas, and our high-tech factories use huge amounts of energy. Can we still lead in green energy?

B2.text: Consider Taiwan's particular position. As a densely populated island with limited land, we are highly exposed to typhoons and rising sea levels, while our advanced manufacturing sector consumes an enormous amount of electricity daily.

stages.language_pattern: present progressive for trends / this causes ...

A2.text: Taiwan is getting hot faster than other places. This is a scary fact. It changes our food and our clean water. We must find a good solution very quickly.

B1.text: The data is worrying, because Taiwan is warming faster than the global average. This changes everything, from the food we grow to the water we drink. Record heatwaves may soon become normal.

B2.text: Recent measurements show that Taiwan is warming faster than the global average, disrupting agricultural yields and freshwater supply alike. Without rapid intervention, today's record heatwaves will gradually become an unwelcome permanent baseline for everyone.

A2.text: Here is the main problem. Taiwan uses too much coal and oil, and these make dirty air. Our chip factories need power all the time. How can we stop the pollution?

B1.text: Here is the main problem. Taiwan still depends on coal and gas, which produce a lot of carbon, while our chip industry needs power every hour. Can we grow and cut pollution together?

B2.text: Our central difficulty is a continued reliance on imported coal and natural gas, while the semiconductor industry, often called our Silicon Shield, requires absolutely uninterrupted power. Economic strength and deep emission cuts therefore appear to conflict.

A2.text: We must ask some hard questions today. Is our high-energy life safe for the future? Can we change to green power fast enough? Students and scientists must answer them.

B1.text: We have to ask some difficult questions. Is this high-energy lifestyle really sustainable, and can we move to green power fast enough? Students and scientists like us have to answer them.

B2.text: We should confront several uncomfortable questions honestly rather than postpone them. Is an energy-intensive lifestyle sustainable in the long term, and can the shift toward renewables outpace the ecological damage we cause?

A2.text: But there is good news. Taiwan made a new climate law. Our goal is Net Zero by 2050. Now companies must pay money if they make too much dirty air.

B1.text: But there is good news. Taiwan has passed the Climate Change Response Act, which sets one clear goal: Net Zero by 2050. Companies that pollute more now pay a higher carbon fee.

B2.text: There has nevertheless been genuine progress worth recognising. Taiwan enacted the Climate Change Response Act, writing Net Zero by 2050 into law, while a national carbon fee now makes heavy polluters pay directly for their emissions.

A2.text: We can see big changes. There are many new wind turbines in the sea, and our wind power is growing fast. Schools and factories also put solar panels on their roofs.

B1.text: Our landscape has changed as well. Offshore wind turbines now stand in the Taiwan Strait, and our wind power is growing quickly. Solar panels have also appeared on school and factory roofs.

B2.text: The landscape itself is being transformed before our eyes. Offshore wind farms across the Taiwan Strait demonstrate how quickly renewable capacity can scale, and rooftop solar keeps expanding across schools, factories and public buildings.

A2.text: People in Taiwan are very good at recycling. We ride the MRT and Ubike every day. Green living is popular now. But is recycling enough? We need bigger changes too.

B1.text: People here recycle carefully, and we use the MRT and Ubike more than ever, so green living has become popular. However, recycling alone is not enough to stop the crisis.

B2.text: Public engagement remains strong, since citizens recycle carefully and rely heavily on public transport systems. Even so, individual habits alone cannot deliver climate stability; only systemic reform actually moves national emissions downward.

stages.source_description: Solutions and STEM Integration (解決方案與 STEM 整合)

A2.text: How can science help Taiwan? We are building smart grids. They use AI to share electricity. This technology stops energy waste and makes our power system work better.

B1.text: How can technology help us? Taiwan is building smart grids that use artificial intelligence to manage electricity. Imagine a brain that knows exactly where power is needed; this cuts a lot of waste.

B2.text: How might technology accelerate this transition further? Taiwan is developing smart grids that use artificial intelligence to balance supply and demand, which reduces waste and raises the efficiency of the entire national power system.

A2.text: Another cool invention is carbon capture. Scientists catch bad air from factory chimneys before it goes into the sky. Then they hide it deep underground. This science really helps.

B1.text: Another innovation is carbon capture. Scientists here catch carbon dioxide from factory chimneys before it reaches the air, and then store it safely underground. It sounds impossible, but it already works.

B2.text: Carbon capture represents another promising frontier for our engineers. They intercept carbon dioxide at industrial chimneys before it enters the atmosphere and store it underground, allowing manufacturing and environmental protection to coexist.

A2.text: Think about our streets. Taiwan is famous for electric scooters. They use batteries, not gasoline. This smart design stops dirty air and loud noise in crowded cities.

B1.text: Think about our streets, where Taiwan is famous for electric scooters with swappable batteries. This clever design reduces both pollution and noise in crowded cities, and other countries are copying it.

B2.text: In urban mobility, Taiwan's swappable-battery electric scooters have become internationally recognised. This locally developed innovation reduces air and noise pollution in dense cities, and it offers a practical template other economies can adopt.

stages.source_description: Implications and Future Challenges (影響與未來挑戰)

A2.text: However, being green is not easy. New technology is very expensive. Small shops worry they cannot pay. How can we help everyone buy green things? Nobody should be left behind.

B1.text: However, going green is not easy, because new technology is expensive and many small businesses worry about the cost. If we are not careful, climate policy will leave poorer families behind.

B2.text: Decarbonisation nevertheless creates real economic friction for smaller companies, because green technology demands heavy investment that they may struggle to afford. The transition must therefore be designed so that vulnerable communities are not penalised.

A2.text: Energy safety is a big debate now. Our tech factories need stable power every hour. But wind and solar need good weather. Should we use nuclear power or gas?

B1.text: Energy security is another serious debate. Our high-tech industry needs stable power day and night, but wind and solar depend on the weather. Should we choose nuclear power or more natural gas?

B2.text: Energy security remains genuinely contested in Taiwan. Precision industry requires absolutely stable power, yet solar and wind generation are intermittent, so choosing between expanded natural gas and nuclear energy stays politically painful.

A2.text: Climate change has no borders. Taiwan has great technology, and we want to share it. Politics can be difficult, but we must work together. A storm hurts everyone.

B1.text: Climate change is a global fight, so Taiwan wants to share its technology with other countries. International politics makes this difficult, but a storm in one country affects all of us.

B2.text: Climate disruption ignores national borders, which means that our response has to be international in scope. Taiwan holds green technology worth sharing, although diplomatic constraints continue to complicate genuine cooperation with partner countries.

A2.text: Finally, we must be careful. Some companies lie about being green. We call this greenwashing. As students, we must check the data and ask about their promises.

B1.text: Finally, we must stay careful about greenwashing, which happens when companies look green but never really change. As students, we should check the data and ask whether promises are actually kept.

B2.text: Finally, vigilance matters a great deal here. Greenwashing allows companies to claim environmental credit without meaningful change, so informed citizens should demand verified data and hold industry and government to the 2050 commitment.

stages.source_description: Conclusion and Call to Action (結論與行動號召)

A2.text: To sum up, Taiwan is doing a good job. We have laws, wind power, and smart technology. We are changing from a dirty island into a green leader.

B1.text: To sum up, Taiwan is on the right track. We now have the laws, the wind power and the smart technology. We are slowly becoming a green leader instead of a carbon-heavy island.

B2.text: To summarise, Taiwan is moving along the right trajectory, supported by new legislation, expanding wind capacity and increasingly intelligent energy systems. The shift from a carbon-heavy economy to a green one is difficult but entirely necessary.

A2.text: Why does this matter to you? Because you are the future. You can study science and invent better tools. You can also save energy at home and speak up.

B1.text: Why does this matter to you? Because you are the future scientists and leaders who can use STEM to invent better solutions. You can also start today by saving energy and speaking up.

B2.text: Why should any of this concern you directly? Because your generation will supply the scientists and policymakers who engineer better solutions, and because public opinion shifts noticeably when informed students decide to speak up.

A2.text: Do not be afraid of the climate crisis. Feel excited to help! Taiwan has smart people and kind hearts. Innovation is our strength. Let us build a clean world.

B1.text: Do not feel overwhelmed by the climate crisis; feel motivated instead. Taiwan has the talent and the determination to lead this change. Let us build a country with clean air and blue skies.

B2.text: Rather than feeling paralysed by the scale of this crisis, allow it to sharpen your ambition instead. Taiwan has the talent and the determination to build a country where clean air is entirely normal.

A2.text: The clock is ticking. The Earth is calling for help. Will you be part of the solution? Taiwan is ready for SDG 13, and so am I. Thank you for listening.

B1.text: The clock is ticking and the Earth is calling for action, so will you be part of the solution? Taiwan is ready for SDG 13, and so am I. Let us start together now.

B2.text: The clock is ticking and the planet demands decisive action, so will you simply observe this transition or help engineer it? Taiwan is ready to deliver SDG 13, and so am I. Let us begin now.
